html:
The Paleo-Inuit, also called Paleo-Eskimo, were the peoples of the Arctic from Chukotka across North America to Greenland before the Inuit arrived. Their first culture had formed by about 3900 to 3600 BCE, and the last, the Dorset culture, had disappeared by about 1500 CE.

Around 2500 BCE they spread fast east across the Canadian Arctic to Greenland, where the Saqqaq culture lived. They lived in small groups in skin tents and hunted seals, musk ox and caribou with finely made small stone tools. The later Dorset people carved small ivory figures of animals and people.

Genetic studies suggest they were a population of their own, not the ancestors of today's Inuit. From about 1000 CE the Thule people, ancestors of the Inuit, spread east from Alaska in the Thule migration and replaced them. Inuit stories of an earlier people, the Tuniit, may remember them. Together they make up the long history of the Arctic marine mammal hunters.
